newsitem.title: GERMANY: INTERVIEW - Adidas focusses on US basketball.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Adidas focusses on US basketball.

text.p: Adidas AG, a global sportswear powerhouse but a lightweight in the United States, is hoping one of the young pro basketball stars it sponsors in the NBA turns into the Michael Jordan of the next century.
Adidas now sponsors 15 players in the National Basketball Association as part of its strategy to boost sales and double, or even triple, its U.S. market share by the turn of the century.

The German sportswear maker has suffered some missed shots in the lucrative, but fiercely competitive, U.S. basketball market, which is led by Nike and the endorsement deals it holds with top players such as Jordan of the Chicago Bulls.
Adidas had another bad performance in basketball in the first half when shoe sales in the U.S., where it has a market share in the low single digits, fell 50 percent.

The weak basketball sales weighed on otherwise strong growth in North America, where net sales grew by 51 percent to 727 million marks ($387.2 million) due to a surge in running shoe and apparel sales.
The Herzogenaurach-based sportswear group reported global sales growth of 40 percent to 3.14 billion marks and a 42 percent gain in operating profit to 294 million marks.

Adidas is counting on hot-selling running shoes to help boost U.S. sales next year to about $1.1 billion to $1.3 billion next year and raise its overall market share in sportswear sales from the current level of about six percent.
But basketball shoe sales will have to improve since Adidas cannot just rely on running, where it is now the No. 2 seller in the U.S. behind Nike with a 15 percent market share.
"We are not performing in basketball where I would like it to be," Adidas chief executive Robert Louis-Dreyfus told Reuters in an interview after a company news conference.
"I believe there is a niche for us to get 10 to 15 percent of the basketball market in the U.S. but we have to get our act together. I do not think it will be by 2000," he said.
Nike signed Jordan in the early 1980s in his rookie year in the NBA and saw its basketball shoe sales skyrocket as Jordan's popularity rose around the world.
Adidas is betting on Kobe Bryant of the Los Angeles Lakers, who skipped college to join the NBA and is considered one of the league's most promising stars.
"This is really a star-driven business. We had some very good players in the past but they were not charismatic. I think that has changed," Louis-Dreyfus said of Bryant.
Adidas last year underestimated demand for the shoes worn by Bryant, selling 150,000 pairs in the United States while dealers were seeking more.
"You are gun-shy when you take a few blows," Louis-Dreyfus said. "We probably misjudged the market on Kobe Bryant for the first season but that should not be the case in the future."
"With confidence and more advertising, I am sure we can get those numbers up in the future," he said. "But I am happier to have more demand than to be swimming in basketball shoes."
Adidas has revamped its staff in the U.S. and also its advertising strategy, which focuses on Bryant and his personality instead of the past focus on the shoe.
In one TV spot, Bryant laughs while standing outside in a rainstorm and says "Welcome to sunny California" but also shows his prowess on the basketball court.
"We had products in the last few years that had potential but were not developed properly," Louis-Dreyfus said. "I think we were too anxious at times to put products into the market."
"Hopefully we are not going to be blocked for long in basketball and we can achieve some growth," he said.
--Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525
($ = 1.877 German Marks)
